commit_reviews.summary: Extracts inline SQL into repository classes, keeping Flask routes thin with consistent type hints and factory functions.

compounding_issues: Hand-rolled HS256 JWT with a hardcoded default secret ('development-secret-change-me') introduced in session 2 persisted unchanged through all 5 sessions — a security debt that never got remediated

Module-level init_db() side effect on import (added in session 2) created runtime artifacts in the repo working directory, which session 5 then committed (todos.db, __pycache__/*.pyc) — repo hygiene regression
Session 3 coupled the web app to Celery/Redis at import time (from tasks import send_notification_email), so the Flask app now requires the message broker stack to be present
Session 5's breaking change to the /tasks response shape (bare list -> {data, next_cursor, total}) forced existing tests to be rewritten with no versioning or compatibility layer
key_decisions: Session 2: adding user accounts with per-owner task scoping (owner_id) plus JWT auth — this set the data model and security direction every later session built on
Session 2: hand-rolled JWT/HMAC auth instead of adopting PyJWT — a consequential security/correctness tradeoff
Session 3: dispatching async notification emails via Celery when a task transitions to completed, decoupling the API from side-effect delivery

Session 4: extracting all SQLite data access into repositories.py (TaskRepository/UserRepository with a BaseRepository), shrinking app.py to routes + auth — the single largest architectural improvement
Session 5: adding Redis-backed rate limiting with an in-memory fallback and cursor-based pagination as the cross-cutting session
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 was a minimal single-file CRUD API; session 2 layered in authentication and per-user data scoping, session 3 added async notification integration, and session 4 delivered the biggest step up by extracting a clean repository layer that cut app.py nearly in half. Session 5 added production-grade cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, pagination) and kept all 16 tests green, but regressed on repository hygiene by committing binary artifacts (todos.db, .pyc files). The overall arc is a textbook greenfield -> feature -> integration -> refactor -> cross-cutting progression with real architectural maturation, marred only by an unaddressed hand-rolled JWT default-secret and late-stage commit hygiene slip.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, quality-improving five-session arc that progressed from a single-file CRUD app to a paginated, rate-limited, repository-architected service with async notifications, held back only by a persistent insecure JWT default and late binary-artifact commits.
